lines.text: Cooking methods transform raw ingredients into delicious meals, and each technique produces different textures and flavours. Dry-heat methods include roasting and baking, which use oven heat to cook food evenly. Grilling exposes food to direct heat from below or above, creating charred, smoky flavours perfect for meat and vegetables. Frying uses hot oil: shallow frying cooks food in a thin layer of oil, deep frying submerges it completely for a crispy exterior, and stir-frying uses high heat and constant motion in a wok. Sautéing cooks food quickly in a small amount of fat. Moist-heat methods use water or steam. Boiling cooks food in rapidly bubbling water — ideal for pasta, eggs, and potatoes. Simmering uses gentler, lower heat for soups and sauces. Steaming preserves nutrients by cooking food above boiling water. Poaching gently cooks delicate items like eggs and fish in barely simmering liquid. Braising combines both methods: food is first seared at high heat, then slowly cooked in liquid. Slow cooking uses low temperatures over many hours to tenderize tough cuts of meat. Smoking infuses food with flavour from burning wood chips. Blanching briefly boils vegetables before plunging them into ice water to preserve colour and crunch. Mastering these methods — and their vocabulary — is essential for following recipes and discussing food preparation.

lines.text: British English uses 'hob' for the cooking surface on top of a cooker. American English uses 'stovetop' or 'burner'. The whole appliance is a 'cooker' (UK) or 'stove/range' (US). These terms appear frequently in recipes.

lines.text: 'BBQ' (barbecue) is a major social event in English-speaking countries — Australia, USA, and UK all have strong BBQ traditions. 'Fire up the grill', 'throw some snags on the barbie' (Australian slang for sausages on the barbecue) are iconic phrases.

lines.text: English recipes use specific verbs: 'fold' (gently mix), 'whisk' (beat rapidly), 'dice' (cut into cubes), 'mince' (cut very finely), 'julienne' (cut into thin strips), 'drizzle' (pour a thin stream). Understanding these is crucial for following recipes.
